```{r library}
library(masque)
```

## Why

`masque` gives an analyst the structure of a confidential table without its
values. Controls are tables derived from a table in which part of the answer is
fixed by construction, so a pipeline can be run where the right reading is
known.

* The **null** control permutes every analysed column, so no analysed column
  is associated with another or with the treatment. It is a smoke test. A
  pipeline that finds strong signal on it has built that signal itself, from the
  outcome or from a column the shuffle left alone. A leak that sits in the
  table, such as a covariate that copies the outcome, is shuffled away with
  everything else, so a quiet null does not clear a pipeline.
* The **negative** control permutes one declared column, by default the
  treatment, within the design strata. Its allocation is random within them
  and everything else is as it was, the outcome included. It is a sham
  assignment: the permuted column is unrelated to the outcome, and any real
  effect it had stays in the outcome as extra noise. Over many replicates the
  share of negatives on which a pipeline rejects is its false-positive rate on
  this table under this allocation. On a randomised experiment, the rank of the
  real result among them is a randomisation p-value.
* The **positive** control adds a declared shift per level to the negative.
  The share of positives on which a pipeline finds it is its sensitivity to a
  clean shift of that size on this table.

In epidemiology a negative control is a variable chosen to share the bias of
the question. These controls are null by permutation and share no bias, so none
of them can show confounding.

Nothing is re-simulated. Each control is a permutation of the table it was
built from, with a shift added for the positive. The design columns and the
missing cells are those of the input, and every column keeps its set of values,
apart from the shifted target of a positive.

## A clone and a declaration

The example is the alpha-design trial shipped with the package: 24
genotypes in 72 plots, three replicates, six blocks of four plots within
each replicate.

```{r trial}
trial <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "john_alpha.csv", package = "masque"))
r <- propose_roles(trial, detect = FALSE)
r <- set_role(r, c("rep", "block"), role = "design", action = "keep")
r <- set_role(r, "gen", role = "treatment", action = "keep")
r <- set_role(r, "yield", role = "outcome", action = "scramble")
r <- set_role(r, c("plot", "row", "col"), role = "id", action = "keep")
m <- mask(trial, r, seed = 1L)
clone <- synthetic(m)
```

The control spec is declared once, before any control exists. It names the
column to permute, the strata to permute it within, the outcome to plant an
effect on, the effect per genotype in units of the outcome's standard
deviation, the number of replicates and the seed. Here the planted
genotype effects are drawn from a normal distribution with standard
deviation 0.5, under the spec's seed, so the same vector is planted on
every table the spec meets.

```{r spec}
spec <- control_spec(
  on = "gen",
  target = "yield",
  effect = list(sd = 0.5),
  strata = "rep",
  n = 19L,
  seed = 2026L
)
spec
```

## The analyst's side: controls from the clone

The analyst holds the clone and its role table, and nothing else. The
controls are derived from the clone, so they disclose nothing the clone
does not.

```{r controls-clone}
ctl <- controls(clone, roles(m), spec)
ctl
```

The print shows the resolved declaration and the planted truth: for each
genotype, the shift in standard-deviation units and the shift in yield
units that the positive control adds to that genotype's plots. The `@truth`
table holds the same, and `@manifest` lists every dataset with its seed.

A small pipeline stands in for the analyst's: an analysis of variance of
yield on replicate, block within replicate and genotype, returning the
p-value of the genotype term.

```{r pipeline}
genotype_p <- function(d) {
  blocks <- interaction(d$rep, d$block, drop = TRUE)
  fit <- stats::lm(yield ~ blocks + gen, data = d)
  stats::anova(fit)["gen", "Pr(>F)"]
}
```

On the clone itself the genotype term is not expected to show, because the
default clone re-simulates yield without a genotype effect. On the null it
must not show. On the negatives it shows at the pipeline's false-positive
rate. On the positives it shows at the rate the pipeline finds the planted
shift.

```{r run}
p_clone <- genotype_p(clone)
p_null <- genotype_p(control_table(ctl, "null"))
p_neg <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl, "negative", i))
}, numeric(1))
p_pos <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl, "positive", i))
}, numeric(1))
data.frame(
  dataset = c("clone", "null", "negative (19)", "positive (19)"),
  p_or_share_below_0.05 = c(
    round(p_clone, 3), round(p_null, 3),
    mean(p_neg < 0.05), mean(p_pos < 0.05)
  )
)
```

The negatives give the pipeline's false-positive rate, and the positives the
rate at which it finds the planted shift. Both describe this pipeline on this
table under these permutations, learned without a single real yield. Another
table with the same design can give other rates.

The construction can be checked as well. The genotype means on a positive
replicate, less those on its negative replicate, are the planted shifts
exactly, because the two share one permutation. This checks the controls, not
the pipeline: raw genotype means recover the shifts by construction, so only an
adjusted estimate can show a fault in the pipeline.

```{r recovery}
neg <- control_table(ctl, "negative", 1L)
pos <- control_table(ctl, "positive", 1L)
recovered <- tapply(pos$yield, pos$gen, mean) - tapply(neg$yield, neg$gen, mean)
planted <- ctl@truth$shift_realised[match(names(recovered), ctl@truth$level)]
all.equal(as.numeric(recovered), planted)
```

The planted size is in units of the yield's standard deviation in the table
at hand. That standard deviation holds the block variance and any real
genotype effect, so a size of 0.5 is not half the noise the pipeline sees.
Read it against the residual of the pipeline's own model:

```{r residual-units}
residual_sd <- function(d) {
  blocks <- interaction(d$rep, d$block, drop = TRUE)
  summary(stats::lm(yield ~ blocks + gen, data = d))$sigma
}
0.5 * ctl@truth$sd_y[1] / residual_sd(clone)
```

## The owner's side: the same spec on the original

The owner runs the pipeline the analyst handed back on the original table,
and on controls derived from the original with the same spec. One thing
changes: the permutations are drawn privately. Here that is an integer given
as `seed`, which overrides the spec's seed; the plan route below uses a 256-bit
key instead. The planted vector still comes from the spec's seed, so the truth
is the same on both sides. A public seed would let anyone who knows the design,
which the clone shares, rebuild every permutation and read the original outcome
out of per-replicate results. An integer has at most 31 bits, so it hides the
permutations only while nothing per-replicate is released.

```{r controls-original}
ctl_owner <- controls(trial, r, spec, seed = 40371L)
p_real <- genotype_p(trial)
p_neg_owner <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl_owner, "negative", i))
}, numeric(1))
p_pos_owner <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl_owner, "positive", i))
}, numeric(1))
```

Each reading is classed by what it estimates before it goes through the owner's
usual output checking. The false-positive rate over the negatives describes the
pipeline under sham assignment. For a test whose null distribution does not
depend on the yields, it says little about them. The rate
at which the positives find the shift depends on the residual variance, so it
tells something about the scale of the real noise. The permutation p-value, the
share of negatives whose p-value is at or below the real one, is the result of
the analyst's test on the real table, and it is checked as a result.

```{r verdict}
data.frame(
  verdict = c(
    "false-positive rate (negatives)", "planted shift found (positives)",
    "permutation p-value of the real result"
  ),
  value = c(
    mean(p_neg_owner < 0.05), mean(p_pos_owner < 0.05),
    (sum(p_neg_owner <= p_real) + 1) / (spec@n + 1)
  )
)
```

The owner's readings describe the pipeline on the real table, and they are the
ones that answer the analyst. The clone's readings are a rehearsal. Here the
two sides read close to each other, within what 19 replicates can resolve.
They need not. The default clone re-simulates yield without the block
structure, so its residual variance differs from the original's. A gap
between the readings is a statement about the clone. Agreement is not a check
on the pipeline, and a rate of zero on both sides agrees while saying nothing.
The same planted 0.5 is
`r round(0.5 * ctl_owner@truth$sd_y[1] / residual_sd(trial), 2)` residual
standard deviations of the pipeline's model on the original and
`r round(0.5 * ctl@truth$sd_y[1] / residual_sd(clone), 2)` on the clone.

The control tables built from the original hold the real values and never
leave. Per-replicate results do not leave either: each replicate is one
more query against the original, and with the permutations known they are
linear equations in the real outcome. The replicate count in the spec bounds
the queries for one pipeline, and every further pipeline or spec run on the
original is another set of them.

## Carrying the spec in a plan

So far the spec has been a separate object. A plan fixes it in advance, with the
roles, and takes it through the boundary. At `mask()` the spec is resolved on
the source and recorded on the recipe. Where a unit or strata are not declared,
the plan picks them: here the replicate, since each replicate holds every
genotype and a block does not. The clone is unchanged by the spec.

```{r plan-mask}
r_plan <- set_role(r, "gen", role = "treatment", action = "alias")
plan <- masque_plan(
  r_plan,
  conditional = "design",
  controls = control_spec(
    on = "gen", target = "yield", effect = list(sd = 0.5), n = 19L, seed = 2026L
  )
)
m_plan <- suppressWarnings(mask(trial, plan, mode = "local", seed = 1L))
recipe(m_plan)@plan@controls$default@strata
```

`conditional = "design"` keeps the design means and block variance and carries
no genotype effect. A real effect moves into the residual, as it does when the
owner permutes genotype for a negative control, so the clone stands in for those
negatives. A fit on this clone does not show the residual of a fit on the
original.

The analyst gets the plan in the clone's own names and labels. `handover()`
writes it to a folder with a collaborate-mode clone, the data card and a note,
and leaves the recipe out. From there the analyst rebuilds the declared controls.

```{r plan-analyst}
analyst_plan <- clone_plan(m_plan)
ctl_analyst <- controls(synthetic(m_plan), analyst_plan)
ctl_analyst@spec@strata
```

The owner passes the same plan with the recipe and the real table. Cleaning is
replayed, a table that does not match the recipe is refused, a spec changed since
`mask()` is refused, and the permutations come from the digest of a key on the
recipe, with no integer seed to search, so the analyst cannot rebuild them.

```{r plan-owner}
ctl_owner_plan <- controls(trial, analyst_plan, recipe = recipe(m_plan))
identical(ctl_owner_plan@seeds, ctl_analyst@seeds)
```

## What a control cannot tell you

* A kept column is structure and is never permuted. Leakage through kept
  columns, ids or row order passes the null.
* The strata should let every level of the column reach every stratum, as
  complete replicates do. Permuting within incomplete blocks leaves each
  block with its own set of genotypes, so part of the real genotype signal
  survives on the negatives, and the false-positive rate reads high or low
  depending on the layout.
* A sequential test depends on the order of its terms. A treatment entered
  before the blocks carries their variance, and its false-positive rate on
  this design is well above nominal. The negatives show this, as they should.
* The negative control reassigns one column under exchangeable allocation
  within the strata. The outcome is unchanged, so a large real effect of that
  column makes the residual on a negative larger than on the original. It
  cannot detect confounding, and on observational data it is a permutation
  test with no randomisation guarantee behind it.
* A planted effect is clean: the same shift for every plot of a genotype,
  no confounding, no interaction. The positives measure sensitivity to a
  clean shift of the declared size, not power against the real effect, and a
  pipeline that is biased under confounding still finds it.
* A shift is added in units of the outcome's standard deviation in the table
  at hand. That standard deviation includes the design variance and any real
  effect, so the same spec plants the same nominal size on the clone and on
  the original while the shift relative to the residual may differ. The
  `@truth` table records the standard deviation used and, as
  `sd_within_strata`, the standard deviation left after the stratum means
  are removed. That figure still holds the effect of `on` and any variance
  within the strata, so it is larger than the residual of a model that fits
  them.
* Nothing is clipped. A negative shift can take a non-negative outcome
  below zero; `control_table()` warns when it does. On a count the shift is
  added, not a change of rate.
* A negative control estimates the size of a test that uses within-stratum
  contrasts, so fit the strata. On this design, with replicate strata, `yield ~
  rep + gen` rejects near 5 percent and `yield ~ gen` rejects almost never,
  because the replicate variance stays in its residual. A shared rate on both
  sides is agreement between them, and zero on both says nothing about
  calibration.
* The null collapses the design means of row-level outcomes, so a mixed
  model sees a different variance structure. Calibrate false positives on
  the negative control, not on the null.
* A pipeline adjusted until its controls read well has been fitted to this
  null and this planted shift. It can still be wrong for every other
  question.

```{r teardown, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
